source.title: Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders Cross-Lingual Performance
source.authors: Zheng Wei Lim; Alham Fikri Aji; Trevor Cohn

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures cross-language representation similarity and reports that alignment is not monotonic with model size: middle-sized models are more aligned than both smaller and larger counterparts. It also compares similarity measures and layers.
record.gate_note: Rows record the cross-lingual similarity curves in Figure 1. Table 2 reports correlations between similarity and accuracy, consistency, and positive transfer; these are not separately rowed here. Logit-lens and steering results are not rows: the former compares latent answer probabilities to language-specific embedding spaces rather than measuring the versions' named alignment, and the latter deliberately induces English-directed processing.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It measures how similar one model's representations of parallel queries in different languages are (CKA and normalized cosine, within a single Gemma 2 or Qwen 2.5 model). It never compares representations across independently trained models, seeds or modalities. This is a related but different construct, so it is recorded under fits_no_version. The paper does not cite or rely on the Platonic Representation Hypothesis or convergent learning.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LLMs are inconsistent across languages because they rely on representations that are dissimilar across languages. Larger models are more accurate, but their representations diverge into language-specific subspaces, while smaller models work in an English-like shared space. Cross-lingual similarity strongly predicts consistency and transfer (Table 2). Steering toward English helps small models but not larger ones.
record.recipe_differences: Measures similarity between language-specific representations within multilingual LLMs using linear CKA and normalized cosine similarity; it does not compare independent models representing the same inputs as in the claim's cross-model formulation.
record.method_sensitivity: Similarity trends vary by metric and layer; the paper also reports different alignment patterns across model sizes and datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Within each family, the middle-sized models (Gemma 2 9B, Qwen 2.5 7B) show the highest cross-lingual alignment of parallel queries. The largest models are less aligned despite better accuracy (Fig. 1). CKA peaks in early layers and declines, while normalized cosine rises in deeper layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a multilingual LLM, alignment of representations of the same content across languages is non-monotonic in model size and depends on the similarity metric and layer.

record.problems: Representation similarities were estimated from 50 randomly sampled parallel queries per dataset. The figures show confidence intervals across language pairs, but the text provides few exact similarity values. The study concerns language alignment within two model families, not cross-model or cross-modal convergence.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 reports Pearson correlations of averaged similarity measures with accuracy, consistency, and positive transfer for each model and task; these numerous association values were not rowed because the rows focus on measured representation similarity itself. Figures 2, 5, 6, and 7 report latent-language probabilities, latent accuracy, or PCA visualizations rather than the cross-lingual similarity metrics catalogued here.

untested.parts: No comparison of representations across independently trained models of different architectures, objectives or data as scale grows.
No cross-model mapping, stitching or relative representations.
No cross-model feature or circuit matching.
Metric dependence of cross-model convergence is not tested. The CKA vs cosine contrast concerns within-model cross-lingual alignment.
Partial cross-model convergence and its causes are not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked every row to V6 and V7. Both versions concern convergence between different models, whereas this paper measures alignment across languages inside one model, so no verdicts are given. The 'partial' states had no clear reference point and the values are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not measure alignment between independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or training data as a function of model scale.
No vision-language models or paired image-caption representations are studied.
The study does not compare seeds or shared features/subspaces across independently initialized networks.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment between models is tested.
The paper does not identify recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.

It compares linear CKA and normalized cosine similarity, multiple layers, and three multilingual task datasets. It does not test out-of-distribution inputs or systematically vary the similarity metrics' settings such as number of neighbours.

It finds non-monotonic cross-lingual alignment across sizes, but does not test whether common training data or objectives cause the observed alignment, nor whether a common model of reality explains it.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Both similarity measures across the three tested datasets and the sampled layer sweeps
reader_labels.reason: Similarity patterns differ by measure and layer: CKA peaks in lower layers and declines, while normalized cosine similarity rises in deeper layers; the text also reports greater alignment for middle-sized models. Rows r01-r36.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma 2 and Qwen 2.5 size comparisons across BELEBELE, mMMLU, and mHellaSwag
reader_labels.reason: Alignment is described as strongest for the middle-sized models (Gemma 2 9B and Qwen 2.5 7B), rather than increasing steadily with scale; the authors say the largest models have more structurally dissimilar language representations. Rows r01-r36.
